description.value: We investigated brain network interactions of smoking self-regulation by employing a real-time smoking (nicotine delivery) decision paradigm and a brain-as-predictor neuroimaging approach.

spans.text: To investigate the neurobiological mechanisms that determine self-regulation of smoking urges when a person encounters stress, we investigated brain network interactions of smoking self-regulation by employing a real-time smoking (nicotine delivery) decision paradigm and a brain-as-predictor neuroimaging approach.

value: we hypothesized that the moment-to-moment brain interactions between executive (dlPFC) and reward (ventral striatum and vmPFC) network areas when encountering a stressor would determine the subsequent trial-by-trial smoking self-regulatory decision outcomes ( ).

spans.text: In other words, we hypothesized that the moment-to-moment brain interactions between executive (dlPFC) and reward (ventral striatum and vmPFC) network areas when encountering a stressor would determine the subsequent trial-by-trial smoking self-regulatory decision outcomes ( ).

description.value: Twenty-five cigarette smokers abstained from smoking overnight and made real smoking decisions during one fMRI session under cognitive stress, emotional stress, and no-stress conditions.

spans.text: We chose this number of trials to maximize statistical power in trial-by-trial level analyses while still ensuring that all the trials could be completed within 1 fMRI session without discomfort (total scanner time of ∼90 min).
